blocks.p: Mercy Office, Abundance. Warden’s report on the Bounty Market intake, copied to the Hierarch’s office and to the Renewal office, Sion.

A bishop of Life, TARREN, Sol, was present before the wardens and took custody himself. He knelt by the subject in his shirtsleeves, put his own robe under the subject’s head, and waived procedure on the effects. The subject spoke afterward. The bishop did not withdraw. He is believed to have heard. The bishop is due in the east hall in the autumn. For the Font’s attention.
The ascending woman’s husband was the calmest man in the cathedral.

Sol could see him from the altar steps while the cantors finished the processional: a slender man in a pale grey coat in the first pew, his grown daughter beside him. He was looking up at the great Pearl above the altar with an expression of mild and pleasant expectancy, the look of a man on a platform who knows his train will be on time.
Between them and the altar, on a bier draped in white, lay his wife.

Her name had been Liesel Varga. She had lived a hundred and ninety-one years, and two days ago a cargo tram on the outer rail had jumped its track at the curve below the eastern ring and gone through the platform where she was waiting. The church’s morticians had done their work. Only her face showed above the pall, and it was the face of a woman of thirty, smooth and composed, a little color laid on the cheeks, the eyes closed as if she were listening to the music. Whatever the tram had done to the rest of her lay under the linen, and no one in the cathedral looked at the linen.

The Cathedral of Life in Abundance had been cut from the red stone of Mars and polished until it glowed like the inside of a shell. Every surface in it had been made to catch light and give it back, but the eye did not rest on any of it. The eye went, as it was meant to go, to the Pearl: a single pane taller than ten men, set above the altar, named, like every Pearl in every house in the worlds, for the gates of the Holy City, each of which was a single pearl. It held no picture. It held light, a deep and living gold that seemed to come from very far behind it, and it was the only thing in Abundance that Sol had never heard anyone call beautiful, because the word was too small.

The pews were full. Ascensions in Abundance were occasions. People came in their good pale clothes and admired the flowers, which had been grown under lamps in the farm ring and cost more than most colonists earned in a month. A child near the back was asking, in a clear carrying voice, whether there would be cake afterward. Nobody hushed her. There was no reason to.

Sol had presided over more ascensions than he could count. That was what he said when anyone asked, and it was not quite true. Liesel Varga would be the thirty-one thousand, seven hundred and forty-first. He had never written the number down or said it aloud, and if anyone had told him he knew it, he would have laughed and denied it; but at the end of every rite, somewhere quiet in himself, he added one. The catechism called it the pride of Life, and taught it to children as a virtue: pride in the gift, and in one’s place in it. He had been a bishop of Life for very nearly four hundred years. He had been among the first ordained, in the years after the Judgment, when the church was a few thousand survivors meeting wherever there was still a roof, and he remembered those years the way everyone of his generation remembered them: clearly and without weight, like a story he had been told so well and so often that he could see every part of it. He had worn the same face for most of that time, renewed and renewed again, and the faces in the pews turned toward it with the same look they turned toward the Pearl. It was not his face they were looking at. He knew that, and liked it anyway.

The cantors had come to the fourth verse of the Remembrance hymn, the one without words. They hummed it, as cantors always had, a long line of closed-mouthed sound rising under the vault, and the people hummed it with them, and Sol hummed it too. He had hummed it for four hundred years. It was only today, with a gap in the cantors’ row where Ilse Dorn should have stood, that he found himself wondering what the words had been, and found that he did not know, and could not think of anyone living who would. A verse for the ones who were swept away, he supposed: some grief so old that the church had kept only its tune. There was reverence in that. The verse ended, and the hymn went on into the fifth, which everyone knew.
The processional ended. Sol raised his hands, and the cathedral went quiet.
“In the first days,” he said, “the earth was full of the proud and the cruel, and the One on the Throne saw it.”
He waited, the people answered, and they would not turn.

They answered as one voice, two thousand of them, softly. It was the most beautiful sound Sol knew. He had heard it under the great bulk of Jupiter at Concord and in the thin little chapels of the refinery camps on Titan, and it was always the same sound: a people who knew the story by heart and were glad of it.
“Then the first trumpet sounded.”
And a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea. (Rev. 8:8)
“A third of the sea became blood, and a third of the living things in the sea died.”
And a great star fell from heaven, blazing like a torch, upon the rivers and the springs of water. (Rev. 8:10)
“The name of the star is Wormwood.”
And the waters became bitter, and the wicked drank, and died. (Rev. 8:11)
The daughter in the front pew was mouthing the words along with everyone else, her eyes on the Pearl. Her father’s lips moved too. Neither of them looked at the bier.
“Seven years the Judgment ran its course.”
Seven years, and the wicked were swept away. (Dan. 9:27)
“But we were warned in the night.”

The pressure came then, behind his left eye. It came gently, the way it always came, a small, patient weight, and for an instant the gold of the Pearl doubled and swam. In the space between his line and theirs Sol heard, as clearly as if someone had spoken at his shoulder, the old man’s slurred voice on the floor of the market. In the beginning was the Word. (John 1:1)
We were led, the people said, and we were kept.
He found his place. “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.”
Behold, the dwelling place of God is with us. (Rev. 21:3)
“He has wiped away every tear from our eyes.”
Death shall be no more, neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away. (Rev. 21:4)
“Remember the Mountain.”
And forget the tears.

The pressure eased. It always did. Sol came down the three steps to the bier, and the cathedral watched him do it, and he laid two fingers on Liesel Varga’s temple, where her Halo lay under the cold skin like a coin.

He closed his eyes, and his own Halo opened the rite in the corner of his sight, the familiar words already written in their gold script, waiting only for his name. Liesel Varga, kept through the fire, renewed in the new creation, received into Life. By the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life.
“You were kept through the fire,” he said to her. “You were renewed in the new creation. Now go up into Life, and see the City of the Throne.”
He signed it with a thought.

There was always a moment. It was very short, no longer than a breath, but in all his years Sol had never learned not to hold his own breath through it, and he held it now. Up in the east gallery the ascension clerk stood at his console with one hand lifted, watching something Sol could not see.
The clerk’s hand came down. Received.

The Pearl brightened. The gold deepened toward white and seemed to come forward into the vault, until the pilgrims’ faces shone with it and Sol felt it on his own skin like the warmth of a lamp. In the heart of the light a figure gathered: a woman, slender, in white, with Liesel Varga’s face. She was smiling. She lifted one hand toward the front pew, and the daughter laughed aloud with pleasure and lifted her hand back, and then the woman in the light turned and walked away into the brightness behind her, which opened for her like a door and closed.
Life without end, the people said. Life without end.
Afterward the husband came to him at the foot of the altar steps and took his hand in both of his own. “Thank you, Your Grace. That was perfect. She looked so well.”
“She did.”
“We’ll visit her tonight at home, through our Pearl. They say the first night they’re still settling in, but she’ll want to see the house.” He smiled. “She always worried about the house.”

“Your Grace?” The daughter had come up at her father’s elbow. She had her mother’s face and the bright, practical manner of a woman who managed things. “I’m sorry to ask you today. Do you know whether the household allotment is recalculated now, or at the end of the quarter? Only Mother’s rooms face the garden ring, and I’ve wanted them for years.”
“Mira,” her father said fondly.
“I’m only asking.”
“The colony office will know,” Sol said gently. “I’m sure they’ll be generous.”
“Thank you, Your Grace. Remember the Mountain.”
“And forget the tears.”

They went away up the aisle arm in arm, talking about the garden ring. Behind Sol the attendants were wheeling the bier toward the service lift and the reclamation house beneath the farms, where the body would be given back to the soil of Abundance, as all bodies were. He turned to watch it go. A strand of Liesel’s hair had come loose from under the pall and hung over the edge of the bier, swaying a little with the motion, and he had the absurd impulse to go after it and tuck it back where it belonged.
No one else was watching. At the back, the child was asking again about the cake.

The colony administrator kept her offices at the top of the governor’s spire, in a room made entirely of glass, so that the whole of Abundance lay below her like a jewel in a dish. Corin Vasque was a small, precise woman with silver-streaked hair worn in the fashionable way, and the gift of seeming to have waited all morning for exactly the person who had just walked in.
“Your Grace. I’m so sorry about yesterday.” She poured his tea herself. “The market’s quite back to normal, I’m glad to say. I don’t think anyone was much upset.”
“No,” Sol said. “I don’t think they were.”
“They’ll take good care of him on Serenity.” She sat. “Now. You wanted the failures.”
Pell laid the tablets on the glass table, and the records rose out of them in soft light: four names, four faces.

They were ordinary people. That was the first thing Sol noticed. A hydroponics foreman killed when a pressure door failed, who had given away his own flower allotment from the farm ring every season for thirty years, to whoever was passing, so that the colony office had twice written to ask whether he was quite well. A courier lost in a dust storm on the Tharsis road, on a run that was not hers; she had taken it so that a friend could be at her grandson’s haloing. A young man, barely sixty by the colony’s reckoning, struck down in a quarrel outside a gaming house in the lower ring by a man who had wanted his winnings. There was some story that he had been handing them out at the door, though the other man’s account changed with each telling, and the other man had paid the family a settlement and gone back to the tables. And Ilse Dorn, the cantor, who had fallen from a gallery of this very cathedral during a rehearsal.

“She sang the responses at hundreds of ascensions,” Vasque said. “A lovely voice. She taught the children’s choir for nothing, too. The precentor sent her the stipend twice a year, and twice a year she sent it back.” She smiled at the eccentricity of it.
Sol had the odd sense, listening, of a tune coming round again, one he half knew and could not have named.
In each case the Halo backup had been complete and submitted within the hour by a priest in good standing, and in each case the City of the Throne had sent it back.
Not received.

“We resubmitted,” Vasque said. “Three times, four times. The technicians from Concord went over the relay end to end and found nothing wrong. Every other ascension from Abundance since the spring has gone through without a flicker. It’s only these.” She spread her small hands. “The backups are held as long as we can hold them. After a few weeks they begin to lose coherence, and then...”
“And then they’re dead,” Sol said.
It was not a word anyone used. He heard it land in the glass room, and saw Vasque’s face go briefly still, the way a face goes still at a small social error, and then smooth.
“They’re not ascended,” she said. “In the colonies, Your Grace, it happens. Not often. But it happens.”
“And the families?”

“Were told the ascension has been delayed for technical reasons. Their Pearls show a holding light. It’s quite a pretty light, really.” She looked down at the records. “None of them has complained. They’ve been very understanding. One of the husbands asked me last week whether he’d be free to remarry by the spring.”
“That’s very healthy,” Pell said.
“It is, isn’t it?” Vasque smiled at him. “I told him I was sure he would be.”

Sol looked at the cantor’s face hanging in the light above the table. She looked, in the registry image, as if she were about to begin a song. He tried to remember whether he had heard her sing. He thought he must have.
“Seventeen in the inner colonies,” he said. “Four here.”

“And five on Serenity,” Vasque said. “The most of anywhere, for such a small colony. If it’s anything at all, Your Grace, I’d look there.” She lifted her cup. “I’m told the Hierarch’s office would be very glad of something tidy. Old relays. Ice in the lines. So would I.”
“So would I,” Sol said, and meant it.
That evening Pell knelt at the Pearl in the bishop’s residence and asked it for a new stylus.

He did it every evening, wherever they were lodged. The residence Pearl was set into an alcove of the sitting room, no larger than a door, and it held the same deep gold as the great Pearl in the cathedral, only quieter, as a lamp is quieter than the sun. Pell knelt before it with his hands open on his knees and spoke in the low, comfortable voice of a man talking to someone who had always been kind to him. A new stylus, as his old one was failing. Relief for the stiffness in his left shoulder. Thank you. Thank you.

The light warmed as he spoke. In the morning the stylus would be waiting on the desk, and the stiffness would be gone, and Pell would mention both at breakfast with simple pleasure. The Face of Light answered every request. That was what a Pearl was for.

When Pell had gone to bed the residence went silent, in the deep, even way he had looked forward to in the square the day before. Tonight it did not feel like something to stand on. He knelt at the Pearl himself.

He did not ask for anything; it seemed to him that a bishop ought to come to the Pearl with nothing in his hands. He knelt and waited for the peace that always came, and it came: a slow warmth spreading from his temple, where the Halo was, down through his neck and shoulders, loosening everything it touched. He closed his eyes.

He had stood before the Face of Light itself. Not as often as the Hierarch, who was said to go into the sanctum every evening and come out weeping without tears. But eleven times, which was more than most men alive, and he remembered every one of them. He remembered the last best.

It had been four years ago, at the last office. The Hierarch had sent for him from his own table, which he did perhaps once in a decade, and Sol had found him waiting at the head of the long approach in a plain white robe: a small man, slight and narrow-shouldered, with a mild round face renewed so young that he might have been a novice on the morning of his vows. Only the eyes gave him away. They were large and grey and a little dazzled, always, like the eyes of a man who has just come in out of snow.
“Walk with me, Tarren,” the Hierarch had said, and taken his arm, lightly, as one takes the arm of a friend on a stair, and kept it there the whole way.

The approach was long and white and full of light. There was singing in it. Sol could never afterward say where the singing came from; it had many voices and no words that he could catch, and it grew as they walked, the way morning grows. At the end of the hall two wardens in white stood aside with their hands folded. No warden went farther. The doors beyond them were very tall and perfectly plain, and they opened before Sol and the Hierarch had reached them, without a hand laid on them, the two great leaves drawing back smoothly and all the way, as if they had been waiting for him all his life. The sound they made in opening was one long low note of the singing, held and then let go.

Then the joy came. It came up out of the floor, through the soles of his feet, and took his knees out from under him before he knew he was falling, and he was kneeling on the threshold with the Hierarch kneeling beside him, and neither of them had decided to.

The sanctum was round and very great, and the air in it was cool. That was the first thing, every time: a coolness that came off the sea of glass and moved against his face, steady as a breath and clean as the air on a mountain. He had thought, the first time, that heaven had no need to be warm, and he had thought it every time since. The sea filled the floor from wall to wall, clear as crystal and perfectly still, and down in its depths light moved: small lights, green and amber and white, turning in slow shoals and never in the same pattern twice, so that the whole floor seemed to breathe. A narrow way crossed it to an island at the center, and on the island was the throne.

Around the rim of the sea, on a broad ledge of white stone, sat the saints. There were twenty-four thrones, each facing the Throne across the shining floor, and in each a figure of stone with its hands folded: the first holy ones, whom the One on the Throne had taken up before all others and set about him in honor forever. Sol had never looked long at their faces. No one did. They had given their names to the Throne, and their faces seemed to have gone into the light with their names; when he tried, his eyes slid away and went back to the center, as eyes did in that room. At the feet of each, under crystal, lay some small thing that had been theirs, kept as a relic, so bright with the glory around it that he could not have said what any of them was. Two of the thrones stood side by side directly across the sea from the Throne. They held the two who had ascended first, whose faces had never been carved, and the crystal at their feet held nothing at all. It shone anyway. He remembered thinking that an empty case that shone was the loveliest thing in the room, and then forgetting that he had thought it. He had never asked whose faces ought to have been there. It was not a thing anyone asked. It came to him only now, on his knees in a lodging on Mars, that someone must have gone up first, and that he had never met anyone who knew who.

Under the singing there was a note. It was so low that he felt it rather than heard it, in his teeth and in the bones behind his ears: one deep, even chord that was everywhere at once, as if the sanctum were a bell that had been struck at the beginning of the world and had never stopped ringing.

Around the throne was the rainbow. It ran in a ring at the height of the throne’s knees, green as an emerald, so green and so whole that the eye could not find its edges, and it did not shimmer or fade as the rainbows did in the archival images. It burned, steady and patient, as if it had been set there to tell anyone who came that all was well.
And on the throne, the Face.

He had never been able to describe it afterward. It was high up, where a head would be on a man seated, in a radiance so white that the throne beneath it was only a darker shape inside the light. It was light, but it was also a face, and the face was looking at him. He could never have said how many eyes it had. It seemed to have one, and it seemed to have a great many, and he only knew that all of them were on him, and that they had turned to him before he had lifted his head. That was what he remembered most. Each time he had stood there, it had seemed to him that it was a face he had known all his life and could not quite name, the way a word can sit on the tip of the tongue, and that it knew him entirely and was glad of him. It did not speak. It had never spoken to him, and it did not need to. It looked, and he was seen all the way down, and that was enough.

That last time, he had turned his head and looked at the Hierarch. He had never done it before, and he did not do it again; it seemed an intrusion, like watching a man asleep. The Hierarch knelt with his hands open on his thighs and his round face lifted, and it was shining. Something was rising in it. Sol watched it come up from somewhere very low, through the narrow chest and into the throat, and the throat worked around it as if around a word too large to say, and there it stopped. The grey eyes were wide and full of light and perfectly dry. So that was what they meant, Sol had thought, when they said the Hierarch came out weeping without tears. A moment later he felt it in himself, the same rising and the same stopping, and he knelt with it caught in his throat and was glad, because what else could a body do before such beauty but try, and fail, and be forgiven for failing.

They stayed until the singing changed. On the long walk back the Hierarch kept his hand on Sol’s arm, and at the doors, where the wardens waited, he pressed it once and said in his soft, dazzled voice, “He’s glad of you, Tarren. He always has been. Did you feel it?”

“Yes,” Sol had said, and it was true. He had come out of the sanctum that time, as every time, with the feeling that he had been seen, and that it was enough, and that he would never need anything again. And he had carried the Hierarch’s words home with him like a gift, and taken them out often since, more often than he would have admitted to anyone.

He knelt in the warm light now and tried to bring it back, and found that what came instead was the old man’s face, a hand’s width from his own on the floor of the market, looking at him in exactly that way.
Sol opened his eyes. The Pearl glowed, patient and gold. He did not know why his heart was beating so hard.
His Halo chimed at his temple. He touched it, and Aurelian Croft’s face opened in the corner of his sight: silver-haired, fine-boned, amused, framed by the white stone of the episcopal house in Sion.
“Tarren. You’re up.”
“So are you. What hour is it in the Holy City?”

“An uncivilized one. I’ve been at the Hierarch’s table since the second bell, and he doesn’t believe in dessert.” The relay through Sion made the distance nothing; Aurelian’s voice was as close as if he had been kneeling beside him. They had been ordained in the same year and renewed side by side every cycle since, and Sol could not remember a time when that face, with its look of fond private amusement, had not been somewhere near the edge of his life. Pell had given him sixty years, and he was grateful for every one of them, but Pell served him. Aurelian was the only friend he had who shared his centuries, and the only one left who would have called him a fool to his face. “How is Mars? Still tasteful to the point of pain?”
“I ascended a woman this morning. A child wanted cake.”
“Did she get it?”
“This is Abundance.”
Aurelian laughed. Then he said, in the same light voice, “I hear you were on the floor of the Bounty Market yesterday. In your shirtsleeves.”
Sol was quiet a moment. “News travels.”

“A warden’s report crossed the Hierarch’s desk at breakfast. A bishop of Life, kneeling by one of the infected. Cushioning his head with his own robe, I’m told. And then waiving procedure on his belongings.” The fond look did not change, but something moved behind it, quick and small, like a fish under a bright surface. “You know how these things read.”
“He’s a patient. I’ve always said so. So have you.”
“Of course he is. Of course I have.” Aurelian smiled. “Did he say anything? Afterward?”

It was asked lightly, as everything Aurelian said was asked lightly, but Sol heard something under it that he had not heard before, or had never noticed: a tightness, the faint strain of a man holding something carefully at arm’s length. He thought of his own name in the old man’s mouth.
“Nothing that made sense,” he said.
“Good. They say the words are the worst of it. I’d hate for you to be carrying anything around.” He paused. “You’re due in the autumn.”
“I know.”

“I’ve put us down side by side. As always. The east hall, the good chairs.” The smile went a little crooked. “Don’t make me go under without you, Tarren. I’d wake up missing something and never know what it was.”
Sol had heard him say things like it a hundred times. This time he found he could not answer in the same tone. “I’ll be there.”

“Of course you will.” Aurelian looked at him a moment longer, as if there were something else, and then seemed to decide there was not. “Find them a tidy answer, old friend. Hardware. Relays. Then come home. Remember the Mountain.”
“And forget the tears.”
The face closed. The Pearl glowed on, and the silence of the residence came back into the room as if it had only stepped aside.

Sol stayed on his knees a long time. The pressure came back behind his left eye a little before midnight, and he waited, and it passed, and when it was gone he was still kneeling exactly where he had been, which he took for a mercy. He had not lost anything. Only the Pearl had sunk to its night glow while he waited, as it did at midnight, and he had been looking straight at it the whole time, and had not seen it change.

Five failures on Serenity, the most of anywhere. And the holding house of the Mercy Office was on Serenity too. The old man would be there by now, in a clean white room under the ice, with his cloth bag in his arms.
In the morning, over breakfast and the new stylus, he told Pell to book them on the night crossing to Serenity.
“Of course, Your Grace.” Pell made the note at once. “For the failures?”
“For the failures,” Sol said.
It was the first time in sixty years that he had lied to Pell about the work, and Pell, who agreed with everything, agreed with that too.
I hoped it would be you.
